entities.summary:
The French and Indian War was a pivotal global conflict in the North American theatre of the Seven Years' War, fought between the British Empire and the French Empire, with their respective Native American allies, from 1754 to 1763.

This war was a turning point in the colonial history of North America, with the British emerging victorious and gaining control of most of the continent. The war was fought on multiple fronts, including the Ohio River Valley, the Great Lakes, and the St. Lawrence River. The conflict involved several key figures, including General Edward Braddock, General James Wolfe, and General Jean-Antoine Lechesne de Marigny.

The war had significant consequences for the indigenous peoples of North America, with many Native American tribes being forced to cede large tracts of land to the British. The war also marked the beginning of the end of French colonial rule in North America. The British victory in the war led to the signing of the Treaty of Paris in 1763, which ceded most of the French colonies in North America to the British.

As French and Indian War leader James Smith recalled, 'This war had been the most dreadful and destructive that ever was in this or any other country.'
